vignette:
Siti, a 25-year-old database administrator, had always been known for her meticulous attention to detail and her warm, friendly demeanor. Her life took a harrowing turn one rainy evening when she was involved in a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. The memory of the moment when her car collided with another vehicle still haunted her; she could vividly recall the screeching tires, the shattering glass, and the feeling of helplessness as everything went dark. Siti had been driving home from a friend’s birthday party, a joyful occasion that had quickly transformed into a nightmare. Now, every time she passed that road, panic would seize her, leading her to take longer routes to avoid the memories that threatened to overwhelm her. Each time the panic struck her as she approached the road, she felt compelled to veer away, believing that avoiding it was the only way to keep the memories at bay and protect her fragile state. This avoidance was a direct response to the overwhelming fear she felt each time she encountered that road; it was as if that stretch of pavement held a power over her, compelling her to do anything to escape the tormenting memories of the crash. If she had concluded that her feelings of panic were valid, she might have faced the road; instead, the avoidance deepened her belief that she was fragile, confirming that she needed to stay away from anything that could provoke those memories. Each time she avoided that road, it reinforced her belief that she was fragile and needed to protect herself from further emotional pain, leading her to seek out even longer routes to work. This avoidance strategy was her way of coping; she stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again. The shadows of that night lingered in her mind; every time she heard a name related to the incident, like "crash," or the name of the road, a wave of panic would wash over her, flooding her with memories she desperately wished to forget. The sound of arguments, whether on television or overheard in the office, would similarly trigger her anxiety, reminding her of the heated arguments she’d had about the accident with her husband, who felt she should have taken a different route. These reminders filled her with an overwhelming sense of guilt, driving home the belief that she was to blame for the accident and could never escape the judgment of others. Each time she encountered a reminder of the crash, it solidified her conviction that the accident was her fault, leading her to feel even more unworthy of understanding and support. Each time she heard those raised voices, it reinforced her belief that she was to blame, solidifying the narrative that others would judge her for her perceived failures, which only intensified her desire to retreat from conversations altogether. Each time the voices of conflict echoed around her, they solidified her belief that she was somehow to blame, convincing her that avoiding conversations was the only way to prevent further judgement. Every argument she overheard pushed her deeper into self-blame, fostering a narrative that she was unworthy of understanding, which fueled her desire to isolate herself even further. As the arguments reminded her of her perceived failures, she became increasingly convinced that opening up about her trauma would only expose her to more judgment, reinforcing her negative self-assessment. This cycle of negative self-appraisal convinced her that sharing her struggles would only lead to more judgment, reinforcing her inclination to retreat from social situations altogether.

In the aftermath of the accident, Siti found herself increasingly withdrawn. She began avoiding physical stressors, convinced that her body was fragile and that any form of exertion might lead her back to that fateful night. Her avoidance extended beyond physical activity; she also distanced herself from friends, who had once played a significant role in her life. Each time she withdrew from a gathering, she felt a quiet assurance that it was her only option, as being around others would only amplify her fears of inadequacy and reinforce her belief that she was weak. Each time she withdrew from a gathering, she felt a quiet assurance that she was keeping her pain hidden, leading her to conclude that the world was a place where she could only be judged, confirming her fears of inadequacy. Siti believed that they wouldn’t understand the depth of her pain, and she feared they might judge her for not handling the trauma better. This conviction kept her silent, creating an isolation that felt justified in her mind, as she concluded that sharing her struggles would only reinforce her inadequacy. In her mind, the longer she stayed silent, the more it confirmed that she was not worthy of support, which perpetuated her isolation and reluctance to engage with others. Her accumulated avoidance strategies, from skipping social gatherings to distancing herself from friends, fed into her belief that she was weak, giving her the impression that she was less capable than others who seemed to cope with their own challenges. She often resorted to self-harm, a misguided attempt to distract herself from the relentless thoughts of the crash. With each act of self-harm, she felt a fleeting sense of relief, yet it only served to deepen her belief that she was unworthy of love and care, as if the pain she inflicted on herself was proof of her fragility. Each act of self-harm seemed to echo her feelings of unworthiness, reinforcing her belief that she was fragile and needed to hide from the world; this only deepened her conviction that she was unworthy of love and care, trapping her in a cycle of pain and isolation. But every time she inflicted pain upon herself, it echoed back in her mind, reinforcing the idea that she was unworthy of love and care, a narrative that seemed impossible to escape. This misguided coping mechanism only deepened her conviction that she was fragile, leading her to believe that if she couldn’t handle her emotions, she must be weaker than others who seemed to cope more easily. Each time she inflicted pain upon herself, she felt a temporary release from the emotional turmoil, but it only reinforced her belief that she was unworthy of love and support.

Siti's negative self-appraisals plagued her thoughts. Her belief that she was to blame for the accident made it seem rational to avoid situations that could trigger her guilt, reinforcing her decision to withdraw from social interactions altogether. She firmly believed that the accident was a result of her actions, a conviction that gnawed at her conscience. The guilt of inaction loomed heavily; she replayed that evening in her mind, tormenting herself with thoughts of how she could have done more to avoid the crash. Every time she found herself in a situation that echoed that night, her mind would spiral into self-blame. In those moments, Siti felt an overwhelming mistrust of people around her, convinced they would judge her for her perceived shortcomings. Her belief that she was to blame for the accident made it easy to conclude that others would see her struggles as further evidence of her inadequacy, reinforcing her tendency to withdraw. The guilt she felt after the accident led her to believe that reaching out for support would only expose her perceived shortcomings, which kept her silent and isolated, convinced that any interaction would only remind her of her failures. As she pulled away from those who cared, the isolation further validated her negative self-assessment, making her feel even more fragile and incapable of handling her emotions. As she continued to isolate herself, it became harder for her to challenge the growing narrative that she was unworthy of help, reinforcing the idea that she was too fragile to seek support. The guilt she carried became a heavy weight, and she felt she could never forgive herself for not being more vigilant.

The relentless cycle of her triggers and maladaptive strategies only deepened her negative appraisals. Each time she was reminded of the accident, her instinct was to retreat further into her shell, avoiding social interactions and any physical stress. This avoidance often led her back to feelings of guilt, reinforcing her belief that she was somehow responsible for what had happened. With every act of avoidance, her mind echoed the sentiment that she was failing to confront her past, further entrenching her belief that she was to blame for the accident and incapable of moving forward. Each time she avoided a social interaction or retreated from a stressful situation, it seemed to confirm her fears; she became convinced that the more she isolated herself, the more evidence she gathered that she couldn’t cope. This growing reliance on avoidance led her to feel increasingly fragile, which in turn deepened her belief that she must be weaker than others who managed to engage with the world around them. The avoidance behaviors she adopted, from skipping social gatherings to withdrawing from friends, only fed into her negative self-assessment, leading her to conclude that any attempt to engage with the world would only expose her fragility. In turn, the self-imposed isolation heightened her anxiety whenever she encountered reminders of the crash, each instance reinforcing her fears and the narratives she told herself. Each time she retreated further into solitude, it only deepened her belief that she was fragile and weak, convincing her that she needed to remain hidden from the world to survive. This growing reliance on avoidance not only intensified her anxiety but also solidified the notion that she was incapable of confronting her past, further entrenching her negative self-beliefs. 

As Siti sat in her therapist's office, she felt a mix of apprehension and hope. She recognized that her habitual avoidance had not only created a trap but had also reinforced the belief that she was unworthy of help, a narrative she desperately wanted to challenge. She recognized that her maladaptive strategies had drawn a map of her trauma around her, marking every place she could no longer go and every interaction she had avoided, cementing her fear that she was forever chained to her past. She realized that her efforts to avoid triggers had created a self-reinforcing cycle of isolation; the more she tried to escape her fears, the more entrenched those fears became, and the harder it seemed to break free from the emotional prison she had built around herself. The weight of her avoidance strategies hung over her, as she recognized that her efforts to escape her triggers had only created new barriers, leaving her feeling trapped in a cycle she couldn't break. It was her husband who had encouraged her to seek help after he noted the despair etched across her face and the distance that had grown between them. His concern was a stark reminder that her isolation had not only affected her but also strained their relationship, amplifying her fears of being judged and reinforcing her belief that she was unworthy of support. What frightened Siti most was the possibility that she might always feel this way, chained to a past that she could neither change nor escape. Yet, deep down, there was a flicker of hope—a desire to reclaim her life and restore the connections she had once cherished. In this moment, she yearned for understanding and the tools to navigate the tumultuous waters of her mind, hoping that perhaps, with help, she could begin to forgive herself and move forward.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not clearly indicate that triggers lead to maladaptive strategies, such as avoidance or self-harm, in a causal manner.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not demonstrate how triggers influence negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: There is no clear causal relationship established showing that negative appraisals lead to maladaptive strategies in the narrative.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette fails to connect maladaptive strategies to negative appraisals, indicating how one influences the other.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The relationship between maladaptive strategies and triggers is not explicitly stated as causal in the narrative.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

vignette_attempts.vignette:
Siti, a 25-year-old database administrator, had always been known for her meticulous attention to detail and her warm, friendly demeanor. Her life took a harrowing turn one rainy evening when she was involved in a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. The memory of the moment when her car collided with another vehicle still haunted her; she could vividly recall the screeching tires, the shattering glass, and the feeling of helplessness as everything went dark. Siti had been driving home from a friend’s birthday party, a joyful occasion that had quickly transformed into a nightmare. Now, every time she passed that road, panic would seize her, leading her to take longer routes to avoid the memories that threatened to overwhelm her. This avoidance was a direct response to the overwhelming fear she felt each time she encountered that road; it was as if that stretch of pavement held a power over her, compelling her to do anything to escape the tormenting memories of the crash. This avoidance strategy was her way of coping; she stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again. The shadows of that night lingered in her mind; every time she heard a name related to the incident, like "crash," or the name of the road, a wave of panic would wash over her, flooding her with memories she desperately wished to forget. The sound of arguments, whether on television or overheard in the office, would similarly trigger her anxiety, reminding her of the heated arguments she’d had about the accident with her husband, who felt she should have taken a different route. Each time she heard those raised voices, it reinforced her belief that she was to blame, solidifying the narrative that others would judge her for her perceived failures, which only intensified her desire to retreat from conversations altogether. Each time the voices of conflict echoed around her, they solidified her belief that she was somehow to blame, convincing her that avoiding conversations was the only way to prevent further judgement. Every argument she overheard pushed her deeper into self-blame, fostering a narrative that she was unworthy of understanding, which fueled her desire to isolate herself even further.

In the aftermath of the accident, Siti found herself increasingly withdrawn. She began avoiding physical stressors, convinced that her body was fragile and that any form of exertion might lead her back to that fateful night. Her avoidance extended beyond physical activity; she also distanced herself from friends, who had once played a significant role in her life. Siti believed that they wouldn’t understand the depth of her pain, and she feared they might judge her for not handling the trauma better. This conviction kept her silent, creating an isolation that felt justified in her mind, as she concluded that sharing her struggles would only reinforce her inadequacy. She often resorted to self-harm, a misguided attempt to distract herself from the relentless thoughts of the crash. Each act of self-harm seemed to echo her feelings of unworthiness, reinforcing her belief that she was fragile and needed to hide from the world; this only deepened her conviction that she was unworthy of love and care, trapping her in a cycle of pain and isolation. But every time she inflicted pain upon herself, it echoed back in her mind, reinforcing the idea that she was unworthy of love and care, a narrative that seemed impossible to escape. This misguided coping mechanism only deepened her conviction that she was fragile, leading her to believe that if she couldn’t handle her emotions, she must be weaker than others who seemed to cope more easily. Each time she inflicted pain upon herself, she felt a temporary release from the emotional turmoil, but it only reinforced her belief that she was unworthy of love and support.

Siti's negative self-appraisals plagued her thoughts. She firmly believed that the accident was a result of her actions, a conviction that gnawed at her conscience. The guilt of inaction loomed heavily; she replayed that evening in her mind, tormenting herself with thoughts of how she could have done more to avoid the crash. Every time she found herself in a situation that echoed that night, her mind would spiral into self-blame. In those moments, Siti felt an overwhelming mistrust of people around her, convinced they would judge her for her perceived shortcomings. Her belief that she was to blame for the accident made it easy to conclude that others would see her struggles as further evidence of her inadequacy, reinforcing her tendency to withdraw. The guilt she felt after the accident led her to believe that reaching out for support would only expose her perceived shortcomings, which kept her silent and isolated, convinced that any interaction would only remind her of her failures. The guilt she carried became a heavy weight, and she felt she could never forgive herself for not being more vigilant.

The relentless cycle of her triggers and maladaptive strategies only deepened her negative appraisals. Each time she was reminded of the accident, her instinct was to retreat further into her shell, avoiding social interactions and any physical stress. This avoidance often led her back to feelings of guilt, reinforcing her belief that she was somehow responsible for what had happened. Each time she avoided a social interaction or retreated from a stressful situation, it seemed to confirm her fears; she became convinced that the more she isolated herself, the more evidence she gathered that she couldn’t cope. The avoidance behaviors she adopted, from skipping social gatherings to withdrawing from friends, only fed into her negative self-assessment, leading her to conclude that any attempt to engage with the world would only expose her fragility. In turn, the self-imposed isolation heightened her anxiety whenever she encountered reminders of the crash, each instance reinforcing her fears and the narratives she told herself. Each time she retreated further into solitude, it only deepened her belief that she was fragile and weak, convincing her that she needed to remain hidden from the world to survive. 

As Siti sat in her therapist's office, she felt a mix of apprehension and hope. She realized that her efforts to avoid triggers had created a self-reinforcing cycle of isolation; the more she tried to escape her fears, the more entrenched those fears became, and the harder it seemed to break free from the emotional prison she had built around herself. The weight of her avoidance strategies hung over her, as she recognized that her efforts to escape her triggers had only created new barriers, leaving her feeling trapped in a cycle she couldn't break. It was her husband who had encouraged her to seek help after he noted the despair etched across her face and the distance that had grown between them. What frightened Siti most was the possibility that she might always feel this way, chained to a past that she could neither change nor escape. Yet, deep down, there was a flicker of hope—a desire to reclaim her life and restore the connections she had once cherished. In this moment, she yearned for understanding and the tools to navigate the tumultuous waters of her mind, hoping that perhaps, with help, she could begin to forgive herself and move forward.
